## Solution

Consider the complex-valued integrand built from the real part of the target. Using
$$\cos\varphi - i\sin\varphi = e^{-i\varphi},$$
we have
$$e^{\cos\varphi}\,e^{i(\varphi-\sin\varphi)} = e^{\cos\varphi - i\sin\varphi}\,e^{i\varphi} = e^{e^{-i\varphi}}\,e^{i\varphi}.$$
Taking real parts,
$$e^{\cos\varphi}\cos(\varphi-\sin\varphi) = \operatorname{Re}\!\Big(e^{e^{-i\varphi}}\,e^{i\varphi}\Big).$$
Hence
$$I := \int_{0}^{2\pi} e^{\cos\varphi}\cos(\varphi-\sin\varphi)\,d\varphi = \operatorname{Re}\!\int_{0}^{2\pi} e^{e^{-i\varphi}}\,e^{i\varphi}\,d\varphi.$$

**Change of variable.** Set $z = e^{i\varphi}$, so $|z|=1$, $d\varphi = \dfrac{dz}{iz}$, $e^{-i\varphi}=1/z$, and $e^{i\varphi}=z$. Then
$$\int_{0}^{2\pi} e^{e^{-i\varphi}}\,e^{i\varphi}\,d\varphi = \oint_{|z|=1} e^{1/z}\cdot z\cdot\frac{dz}{iz} = \frac{1}{i}\oint_{|z|=1} e^{1/z}\,dz.$$

**Residue computation.** The function $e^{1/z}$ has an essential singularity at $z=0$. Its Laurent expansion about $0$ is
$$e^{1/z} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!\,z^{n}} = 1 + \frac{1}{z} + \frac{1}{2!\,z^{2}} + \cdots.$$
The residue at $z=0$ is the coefficient of $z^{-1}$, namely
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=0} e^{1/z} = \frac{1}{1!} = 1.$$

By the residue theorem,
$$\oint_{|z|=1} e^{1/z}\,dz = 2\pi i\cdot \operatorname{Res}_{z=0} e^{1/z} = 2\pi i.$$
Therefore
$$\int_{0}^{2\pi} e^{e^{-i\varphi}}\,e^{i\varphi}\,d\varphi = \frac{1}{i}\cdot 2\pi i = 2\pi,$$
which is purely real. Taking the real part (which leaves it unchanged),
$$I = \operatorname{Re}(2\pi) = 2\pi.$$

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{\cos\varphi}\cos(\varphi-\sin\varphi)\,d\varphi = 2\pi.}$$
